power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 7 detected *p* values.

table.formatted: Across the 685 external participants, the AUC was 0.56 (95% CI, 0.51-0.62; P = .03) (Figure <ref type="figure">1A</ref>).
table.expanded: Across the 685 external participants, the AUC was 0.56 (95% CI, 0.51-0.62; P = .03) (Figure 1A).

The MRI score did not predict transition better at higher COGDIS or SIPS positive scores (both q = .82) but did at higher SIPS negative scores (P = .049), without surviving correction (q = .15; eFigures 7 and 8; eTable 7).

Within NAPLS-3, this interaction was nominally significant (P = .03), with an AUC of 0.58 at or above and 0.44 below the median SIPS negative score, as in ZInEP (0.72 vs 0.34) but not PRONIA (0.74 vs 0.72; eTable 6).
Participants who developed psychosis had, if anything, more negative symptoms in NAPLS-3 than in PRONIA (P = .17; eTable 6).
Within NAPLS-3, score offsets among the 9 sites were small (≤0.15 SD; P = .99), and the within-site AUC was 0.54 (95% CI, 0.46-0.61).
Combined, the external separation was 0.64 SD smaller than in PRONIA (95% CI, 0.16-1.12; P = .009).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "P < .05", Text = "Two-sided P < .05 was considered nominally significant, and Benjamini-Hochberg q values are reported within the families listed in eTable 13."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: Participants who developed psychosis had, if anything, more negative symptoms in NAPLS-3 than in PRONIA (P = .17; eTable 6).
Within NAPLS-3, score offsets among the 9 sites were small (≤0.15 SD; P = .99), and the within-site AUC was 0.54 (95% CI, 0.46-0.61).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = .17", "P = .99"), Sentence = c("Participants who developed psychosis had, if anything, more negative symptoms in NAPLS-3 than in PRONIA (P = .17; eTable 6).", "Within NAPLS-3, score offsets among the 9 sites were small (≤0.15 SD; P = .99), and the within-site AUC was 0.54 (95% CI, 0.46-0.61)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
